## Introduction

In this seven-minute overview, we start from the report you just
updated. We work out what a colleague would need to rerun it, then see
how a GitHub release and an archived Zenodo record keep those materials
together and citable. We finish with what to do when the data cannot
be shared.

**Question for the room.** Allow about 30 seconds. Think of the report
you just rendered. What would a colleague need to rerun it exactly and
get the same numbers?

## Decide what to archive {#decide-what-to-archive}

Allow about two minutes. Open `workspace/report.html`. Each part of it
points to files a colleague would need.

| In your report | Files that support it | Where they go |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Methods and results | `workspace/report.qmd` and the `meta-summary.csv` it reads | Track the report source. Attach the summary and the rendered HTML. |
| Pipeline script MD5, variance estimator, and interval method | `workspace/_targets.R`, plus the support and preparation scripts it relies on | Track. |
| Upstream snapshot, raw and selected input MD5s, and inclusion rule | The data source and upstream notice in `data/raw/`, and the dataset metadata | Track. Attach any FAIR assessment record. |
| Dataset and predictive model pin versions | `analysis-data-version.txt`, `dataset-versions.csv`, `predictive-model-version.txt`, and the pins | Attach the version files. Attach the pins if permitted and needed to preserve the exact stored versions. |
| R and *meta* versions | `renv.lock`, the Dockerfile or image reference, and the session record | Track the lockfile and Dockerfile. Attach the session record. |

Track the source that recreates the outputs. Attach the generated
outputs and records that show what this particular run produced. The
source can rebuild them, but an archive keeps the exact copies behind
a reported result.

In this exercise your edits are in `workspace/`. Move the exact source
files into a tracked location before tagging a release of your own project.
Use the [export checklist](09_discussion.qmd#export-work) to collect the
session's outputs. An existing workshop release cannot contain work
you created after it was tagged.

The report records the input checksum and filter so a reader can
recreate the input even if rebuilding the board gives the pin a new
identifier. The predictive model pin records the training version and
checksum. Retain the upstream notice if you include the bundled MIT
teaching snapshot. Check reuse terms separately for other data or
models before depositing them.

## Releases on GitHub {#archiving-releases}

Allow about one minute. A Git commit identifies a repository revision.
A GitHub release gives a tagged revision a name and a place for release
notes and attached files. Zenodo can archive a copy of selected files
and issue a DOI. An archive makes the cited files available under the
access conditions of that record [@zenodo-reserve-doi].

One release ties your pipeline, report source, lockfile, and metadata
together at one tagged revision. A reader can then retrieve that exact
combination rather than the repository's latest state. In the workshop
repository, preparing a release follows the steps we have used
throughout the session:

1.  Record the changes in `CHANGELOG.md` and commit that entry.
2.  Tag the commit and publish a release with notes on the
    [releases page](https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/releases).
3.  Publishing the release builds and pushes the RStudio image first.
    After it succeeds, the Binder image is built and pushed from the same
    revision. With the Zenodo integration enabled for the repository,
    Zenodo also archives the tagged files.

Check the files in each new archive. If an attached output should be
preserved but is missing, add it to the deposit.

## Inspect a Zenodo record

Allow about two minutes. An archive exposes these materials so a reader
can find them without asking you. As an example, open the workshop's
Zenodo record [@workshop-zenodo].
Find the creators, access conditions, the ZIP of the archived revision,
and the list of versions. Each archived release has its own version DOI.
The concept DOI, `10.5281/zenodo.24342489`, represents all versions and
opens the latest version. Cite the workshop using this concept DOI from
`CITATION.cff`. Include the GitHub release tag when you need to identify
the exact workshop files you used.
[Workshop archive](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24342489) ·
[GitHub releases](https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/releases)

The workshop has three connected locations:

| Resource | Role |
| --- | --- |
| [Workshop website](https://jbris.github.io/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/) | Read the published workshop materials. |
| [GitHub repository](https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r) | Find the source files, history, and releases used to publish the site. |
| [Zenodo archive](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24342489) | Find and download the archived releases. |

Each version's related identifier points to the GitHub release tag it
archives. The live website can change as the project changes. Record
the tag that identifies the files behind a particular result. New
releases add version records under the same concept DOI.

This answers the question left open in the
[FAIR demonstration](03_data_documentation.qmd#metadata-checkpoint).
There, the assessor found the title and licence only when the
instructor supplied a separate metadata URL. Zenodo registers the
record's metadata with its DOI, and the DOI resolves to a landing page
that shows the metadata and files. A reader or a tool can start from
the identifier alone. As a follow-up, pass the concept DOI to
`rfair::assess_fair()` and check what the repository exposes. That
assessment describes the version the DOI resolves to on the day you
run it.

## When the data cannot be shared

Allow about one minute. Open science can include restricted-access
data: you can share the methods, code, metadata, and access
conditions while restricting the original observations.

Synthetic data generated with *synthpop* can help others test whether
a workflow runs. It does not let them verify findings computed from
inaccessible originals, and ordinary synthesis is not a privacy
guarantee. A differential privacy claim requires a validated mechanism
and privacy accounting [@near2021-synthetic-data]. The
[supplementary synthetic data exercise](10_synthetic_data.qmd) works
through an example after the workshop.

## Checkpoint {#zenodo-checkpoint}

You can list the files a colleague needs to rerun your report and say
which belong in the tagged source and which to attach. You can connect
a cited archive to a specific release, distinguish its version DOI from
the GitHub release tag and the concept DOI, and explain how publishing
a release produces a new Zenodo archive. Use the concept DOI to cite
the workshop and cite the original review separately for the study data.

We finish with questions and discussion.
[Questions and discussion](09_discussion.qmd)

## After the workshop: archive your own releases {#zenodo-github-integration}

To archive releases of your own repository, follow Zenodo's
[Enable a repository guide](https://help.zenodo.org/docs/github/enable-repository/):

1.  Connect your GitHub account to Zenodo if it is not already linked.
2.  In Zenodo's profile menu, select **GitHub**.
3.  Select **Sync now** to refresh the list of repositories.
4.  Find the repository you maintain and enable its slider.
5.  Refresh the page and check that the repository is enabled.

Once connected, publishing a new GitHub release triggers automatic
archiving in Zenodo. Inspect the resulting version record, its DOI,
metadata, and downloadable files after each release. The **Sync now**
control refreshes the repository list; published releases are the
events that create new archives.
